subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which process of coastal erosion involves waves picking up sand and pebbles and hurling them against the cliff, wearing it away?
options: Abrasion (corrasion)
Attrition
Solution (corrosion)
Hydraulic action
questions.explain: Abrasion, also called corrasion, is when waves fling sediment against the cliff face, grinding it away.

questions.q: What is hydraulic action?
options: The force of water and compressed air forcing open cracks in the rock
Rocks colliding and breaking into smaller, rounder pieces
Weak acids in seawater dissolving rock such as chalk
Sediment carried along in solution by the sea
questions.explain: Hydraulic action occurs when breaking waves force water and trapped air into cracks, prising the rock apart.

questions.q: Attrition is best described as...
options: Rocks and pebbles colliding and becoming smaller, rounder and smoother
Waves compressing air in joints in the cliff
Chemical solution of limestone by seawater
The transport of sediment along the coast
questions.explain: Attrition wears transported material down over time as pieces knock together and lose their edges.

questions.q: In longshore drift, the swash carries sediment up the beach at an angle, but the backwash returns it straight down the slope. What causes this straight-line backwash?
options: Gravity
The prevailing wind
The rising tide
The Coriolis effect
questions.explain: The backwash flows directly down the steepest slope under gravity, producing the zig-zag movement of longshore drift.

questions.q: Which set of characteristics correctly describes constructive waves?
options: Low height, long wavelength, strong swash and weak backwash
High height, short wavelength, strong backwash and weak swash
High height, long wavelength, strong swash and strong backwash
Low height, short wavelength, weak swash and strong backwash
questions.explain: Constructive waves have a powerful swash that deposits material, building up the beach.

questions.q: Why do destructive waves tend to erode and narrow a beach?
options: Their strong backwash drags material back out to sea
Their strong swash pushes material up the beach
They carry a large dissolved load
They only occur at low tide
questions.explain: Destructive waves are steep and frequent with a dominant backwash that removes sediment from the beach.

questions.q: Freeze-thaw weathering is an example of which type of weathering?
options: Mechanical (physical) weathering
Chemical weathering
Biological weathering
Coastal erosion
questions.explain: Water repeatedly freezing and expanding in cracks physically breaks the rock apart without changing its chemistry.

questions.q: A section of cliff made of saturated clay collapses along a curved surface, leaving a rotated block. Which type of mass movement is this?
options: Slumping (rotational slip)
Rockfall
Soil creep
Abrasion
questions.explain: Slumping occurs when saturated clay slides along a concave, curved slip plane.

questions.q: A discordant coastline produces headlands and bays because...
options: Bands of hard and soft rock lie at right angles to the coast and erode at different rates
Bands of rock run parallel to the coast
The whole coastline is made of the same resistant rock
Longshore drift deposits sediment unevenly
questions.explain: Softer rock erodes faster to form bays, while resistant rock is left protruding as headlands.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence in which erosional features develop on a headland?
options: Crack, then cave, then arch, then stack, then stump
Stump, then stack, then arch, then cave
Cave, then stack, then arch, then crack
Arch, then cave, then crack, then stump
questions.explain: Erosion widens a crack into a cave, then an arch, which collapses to leave a stack that is finally reduced to a stump.

questions.q: How is a wave-cut platform formed?
options: A wave-cut notch is eroded at the cliff base, the cliff collapses and retreats, leaving a gently sloping rocky platform
Deposition of sediment builds up a flat area at the base of the cliff
A river deposits sediment where it meets the sea
Longshore drift transports material along the shore
questions.explain: Repeated undercutting and cliff retreat leaves behind the exposed rocky platform at the base of the cliff.

questions.q: Why does a spit often have a recurved (hooked) end?
options: A change in the prevailing wind direction curves the end landward
Rivers push sediment back towards the land
Destructive waves erode the tip
Tidal currents deposit sediment out to sea
questions.explain: Occasional winds from a different direction curl the end of the spit round towards the shore.

questions.q: What is a tombolo?
options: A bar of sand or shingle that joins an island to the mainland
A ridge of sediment that encloses a lagoon across a bay
A beach that forms in a sheltered bay
A steep-sided river valley drowned by the sea
questions.explain: A tombolo forms when a spit grows out from the coast to connect an offshore island to the mainland.

questions.q: A bar is a depositional landform that...
options: Extends across a bay, often trapping a lagoon behind it
Joins an island to the mainland
Projects out from a headland into deep water
Forms a gently sloping rocky platform
questions.explain: A bar forms when a spit grows right across a bay, cutting off a lagoon behind it.

questions.q: A seaside resort is losing its beach because longshore drift is moving sand along the coast. Which hard-engineering structure would best trap the sand and keep the beach?
options: Groynes
A sea wall
Beach nourishment
Managed retreat
questions.explain: Groynes are barriers built at right angles to the shore that trap sediment moving by longshore drift, keeping the beach.

questions.q: How does a modern recurved sea wall protect the coast?
options: It reflects wave energy back out to sea and prevents erosion of the land behind
It traps sediment moving along the coast
It adds new sand to widen the beach
It allows the sea to flood low-lying land
questions.explain: The curved face deflects wave energy seawards, protecting the land behind, although sea walls are expensive to build and maintain.

questions.q: After a town installs groynes, the next stretch of coast downdrift begins to erode much faster. Why?
options: The groynes starve the downdrift coast of sediment by trapping it updrift
The groynes increase the tidal range
The groynes create more constructive waves
The groynes cause the sea level to rise locally
questions.explain: By trapping sediment, groynes reduce the supply reaching beaches further along, leaving them less protected and more easily eroded.

questions.q: Beach nourishment is an example of which approach to coastal management?
options: Soft engineering
Hard engineering
Sub-aerial weathering
Mass movement
questions.explain: Beach nourishment adds sand or shingle to a beach and works with natural processes, making it a soft-engineering method.

questions.q: A council owns a stretch of low-value farmland behind an eroding coast and cannot afford expensive defences. Which strategy lets the sea flood the land and create salt marsh as a natural buffer?
options: Managed retreat (managed realignment)
Building a sea wall
Rock armour
Groynes
questions.explain: Managed retreat abandons defences and lets low-value land flood, creating salt marsh that absorbs wave energy cheaply.

questions.q: Along a coastline of alternating hard limestone and soft clay, which rock is worn away most rapidly, forming bays?
options: The soft clay, as it is less resistant to erosion
The hard limestone
Both erode at exactly the same rate
Neither rock is eroded
questions.explain: Less resistant rock erodes faster to form bays, while the harder, more resistant rock is left protruding as headlands.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Geography (4GE1) specification; Coastal Environments
